Foreword
Diabetes presents a significant global health challenge, affecting millions worldwide and contributing
to premature mortality and morbidity.

metadata.title: Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control: The prevalence of diabetes is increasing globally and is
among the top 10 leading causes of death. In addition, diabetes is a major cause of blindness, kidney
failure, heart attacks, stroke and lower-extremity amputation leading to debilitating complications. Much of the burden caused by diabetes can be prevented with evidence-based, individual-level and
population-level interventions. and its morbidity and mortality burden. The WHO Global Diabetes Compact, launched in 2021, is
a central focus of these efforts. The Compact has the vision of reducing the risk of diabetes and
ensuring that all people who are diagnosed with diabetes have access to equitable, comprehensive,
affordable and quality treatment and care. The work undertaken as part of the Compact will also
support the prevention of type 2 diabetes from obesity, unhealthy diet and physical inactivity. One
of the key components of the Compact is to strengthen the monitoring and evaluation of diabetes
responses through country-level surveillance and monitoring systems. The Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control builds on the WHO global
monitoring framework on noncommunicable diseases with diabetes-related targets, endorsed
by the World Health Assembly in May 2013, as well as the recently adopted five global diabetes
coverage targets in 2022. The proposed diabetes indicators in this guidance reflect multiple
domains, including health system determinants, service delivery, risk factor control, and outcome
and impact.

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control: The indicators were designed to be relevant to people living with diabetes and the
general population. Robust diabetes monitoring indicators are important because they provide insights into where
we are and where we need to go. Beyond measuring progress, they can also help to ensure
accountability—guiding us towards a future with improved life for people with diabetes. Let us
build this future together. Dr Jerôme Salomon
Assistant Director-General

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control: Funding from The Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust is gratefully acknowledged. vii
Disclosure of interests
All external collaborators who acted in their individual capacity submitted to WHO a declaration of
interest disclosing potential conflicts of interest that might affect, or might reasonably be perceived
to affect, their objectivity and independence in relation to the development of the global monitoring
framework for diabetes prevention and control. WHO reviewed each of the declarations related
to professional undertakings on pharmacological and nutritional management of diabetes and
concluded that none could give rise to a potential or reasonably perceived conflict of interest related
to the scope of the diabetes monitoring framework.

Purpose | To assess the availability of governance mechanisms for diabetes prevention
and control at national level.
Definition | Country has a national diabetes prevention and control plan developed/
updated within the past 5 years and the plan is currently implemented.
● A national diabetes prevention and control plan includes a set of specific
strategic actions to be taken to achieve the goals of the national diabetes
prevention and control programme. The plan may be an independent
diabetes prevention and control plan or part of a comprehensive national
plan for noncommunicable diseases.
Numerator | Not applicable
Denominator | Not applicable
Method of estimation | Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Does the country have a national
plan that includes prevention, early detection, treatment and/or care for
diabetes?” and needs to provide a copy of the plan and the latest report on the
implementation of the plan.
Existence of the plan is validated by examining the plan document and
implementation is validated by examining the latest report detailing the
execution of at least one strategic action outlined in the plan.
The indicator is considered “Yes” if the country has a national diabetes
prevention and control plan developed/updated within the past 5 years and the
plan is currently being implemented.
The indicator is considered “Partially yes” if the country has a national diabetes
prevention and control plan developed/updated within the past 5 years, but it is
not currently being implemented.
The indicator is considered “No” if the country does not have a national diabetes
prevention and control plan developed/updated within the past 5 years.
Disaggregation | Type of diabetes included in the plan
Sources of data | NCD country capacity survey, other survey, country report
Limitations/comments | An acceptable minimum number of strategic actions completed according to
plan must be defined at every evaluation period to consider the plan as currently
implemented.

NCD country capacity survey [website]. Geneva: World Health Organization;
2023 (https://www.who.int/teams/ncds/surveillance/monitoring-capacity/
ncdccs, accessed 26 May 2024).

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 31): Indicator name | Existence and enforcement of health taxes on alcoholic beverages, tobacco,
sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed food, foods high in saturated
fats, trans fats, free sugars and/or salt
Purpose | To assess the availability of governance mechanisms for reducing risk factors for
diabetes and diabetes-related complications.
Definition | Country has adopted health taxes on one or more of the following items:
alcoholic beverages, tobacco, sugar-sweetened beverages, foods high in
saturated fats, trans fats, foods high in free sugars, foods high in salt, and these
health taxes are being enforced.
● Health taxes are excise taxes levied on products that have a negative
public health impact, for example, tobacco, alcohol and other non-
alcoholic beverages and food products high in sugar, saturated fats, trans
fats and/or salt.
Numerator | Not applicable
Denominator | Not applicable
Method of estimation | Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Has the country adopted health
taxes on alcoholic beverages, tobacco, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-
processed foods, foods high in saturated fats, trans fats, free sugars and/or salt?”,
and needs to provide a copy of the tax policy/legislation and the latest report on
enforcement of health taxes.
Existence of health taxes is validated by examining tax legislation documents
and implementation is validated by examining the latest report(s) detailing the
enforcement of health taxes.
The indicator is considered “Yes” if the country has adopted health taxes
on at least one type of forementioned products and the health taxes are
being enforced.
The indicator is considered “Partially yes” if the country has adopted health taxes
on at least one type of forementioned products, but the health taxes are not
being enforced.
The indicator is considered “No” if the country has not adopted health taxes on
at least one type of forementioned products.
Disaggregation | Type of product, administrative level (district, provincial, or national)
Sources of data | NCD country capacity survey, other survey, country report
Limitations/comments | None
Related links | WHO Noncommunicable disease surveillance, monitoring and reporting:
NCD country capacity survey [website]. Geneva: World Health Organization;
2023 (https://www.who.int/teams/ncds/surveillance/monitoring-capacity/
ncdccs, accessed 26 May 2024).

Organization; 2024 (https://www.who.int/data/gho/data/themes/health-taxes,
accessed 26 May 2024).

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 32): Indicator name | Existence of national guidelines for diabetes management
Purpose | To assess the availability of governance mechanisms for diabetes management.
Definition | The country has evidence-based national guidelines, protocols, standards, or
technical guidance for diabetes management in primary health care settings,
developed/updated within the past 5 years.
● National guidelines, protocols, standards or technical guidance are
information products endorsed by the ministry of health containing
recommendations for clinical management/practice.
Numerator | Not applicable
Denominator | Not applicable
Method of estimation | Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Does the country have evidence-
based national guidelines, protocols, standards, or technical guidance for
diabetes management in primary health care settings?” and needs to provide
a copy of the national guidelines and the latest report on enforcement of
health taxes.
Existence of evidence-based national guidelines, protocols, standards or
technical guidance is validated by examining documents that outline the
scientific steps that were taken to develop the national guidelines, protocol,
standards or technical guidance.
Disaggregation | Type of diabetes, type of services (e.g. diagnosis, treatment, diabetic foot
management, retinopathy management), type of diabetes complications
Sources of data | NCD country capacity survey, other survey, country report
Limitations/comments | None
Related links | WHO Noncommunicable disease surveillance, monitoring and reporting:
NCD country capacity survey [website]. Geneva: World Health Organization;
2023 (https://www.who.int/teams/ncds/surveillance/monitoring-capacity/
ncdccs, accessed 26 May 2024).

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 33): Indicator name | Referral system for diabetes management
Purpose | To assess the availability of referral and back-referral systems for clinical services
for advanced diabetes.
Definition | The country has a clearly defined and well-established functional referral
and back-referral system for diabetes management, facilitating the seamless
transition between primary care, secondary and tertiary care.

Denominator | Not applicable
Method of estimation | Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Does the country have a clearly

and tertiary care for diabetes management?” and needs to provide a copy of
relevant documents about the referral system.
Existence of a clearly defined, well-established functional referral system is
validated by examining documents that outline mechanisms for referral from
primary care to secondary and tertiary care, as well as feedback mechanisms
from higher to lower levels of care.
Disaggregation | Type of diabetes
Sources of data | NCD country capacity survey, other survey, country report
Limitations/comments | None

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 34): Indicator name | Inclusion of insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose self-
monitoring in national health benefit package
Purpose | To assess integration of insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose self-
monitoring into national health benefit packages.
Definition | Country has a national health benefit package that includes insulin, insulin
delivery devices and blood glucose self-monitoring.
Health benefit packages define the high priority services in a country that should
be made available to all citizens from public funds.
Numerator | Not applicable
Denominator | Not applicable
Method of estimation | Country can respond “Yes” to the question “Does the country have a national
health benefit package that includes insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood
glucose self-monitoring?” and needs to provide a copy of the national health
benefit package.
Inclusion of insulin and insulin delivery devices in the national health benefit
package is validated by examining the national health benefit package document
for insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose self-monitoring coverage.
The indicator is considered “Yes” if the country has a national health benefit
package that includes insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose
self-monitoring.
The indicator is considered “Partially yes” if the country has a national health
benefit package that includes either insulin or insulin delivery devices or blood
glucose self-monitoring but not all.
The indicator is considered “No” if the country has a national health benefit
package, but it does not include insulin, insulin delivery devices or blood glucose
self-monitoring.
Disaggregation | Component of the indicator (insulin or insulin delivery devices or blood glucose
self-monitoring), type of diabetes, type of insulin, level of reimbursement (fully
reimbursed or partially reimbursed), age group of people who are included in the
benefit package, administrative level (national provincial/state/region or district).
Sources of data | NCD country capacity survey, other survey, country report (national health
benefit package list)
Limitations/comments | None
Related links | Keeping the 100-year-old promise: making insulin access universal.

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 35): Indicator name | Insulin, its delivery devices, and blood glucose self-monitoring affordability
Purpose | To assess the affordability of insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose
self-monitoring.
Definition | Country has affordable insulin, insulin delivery devices and blood glucose self-
monitoring for people with diabetes. Affordability means that the monthly
expenses for people living with diabetes or their families, including expenditures
on basic needs represented by national poverty line (NPL), do not exceed the
minimum wage for the lowest paid government sector worker (LPGW).
Numerator | Not applicable
Denominator | Not applicable
Method of estimation | The indicator is considered “Yes”, that is, affordable, if:
[(NPL +monthly cost for insulin, insulin devices and blood glucose self-
monitoring to person with diabetes) /LPGW wage] ≤1
Disaggregation | Type of diabetes, type of insulin, type of insulin delivery device, type of blood
glucose self-monitoring.
Sources of data | Country report, survey, national health insurance claims database
Limitations/comments | A population-weighted average can be used to address differences in prices,
wages and size of population at sub-national levels.
When estimated expenses and wages are derived from different years, general
inflation rate and health care inflation rate must be included in the calculation.
Related links | Keeping the 100-year-old promise: making insulin access universal.
Geneva: World Health Organization; 2021 (https://apps.who.int/iris/
handle/10665/348384).
SDG indicator metadata. New York: United Nations; 2019 (https://unstats.un.org/
sdgs/metadata/files/Metadata-03-0B-03.pdf, accessed 26 May 2024).

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 36): Indicator name | Availability of trained health care staff for diabetes management
Purpose | To assess the availability of high-quality services for diabetes management.
Definition | Proportion of health facilities in which staff have been trained in the latest WHO
or national guidelines on diabetes clinical management.
Numerator | Number of health facilities in which staff have been trained in the latest
WHO or national guidelines on diabetes clinical management during the
reporting period.
“Staff” refers to physicians or other nationally authorized health professionals for
diabetes management. A multidisciplinary care team for diabetes management
may include the following:
● cardiologist
● diabetes nurse
● endocrinologist
● general practitioner
● homecare nurse
● nephrologist
● nutritionist
● ophthalmologist
● physiotherapist
● podiatrist
Denominator | Total number of health facilities
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Facility level of care type, provider ownership type (public/private), facility
location type (urban/rural), training topic, type of health professional
Sources of data | Health facility report, health workforce information system or survey
Limitations/comments | Frequency of training depends on the date of the last version of WHO or national
guidelines, as well as the staff turnover at the health care facility.
Related links | HEARTS-D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes. Geneva: World Health
Organization; 2020 (https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/331710).

primary health care. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2020 (https://iris.who.
int/handle/10665/334186).

World Health Organization; 2021 (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/
harmonized-health-facility-assessment-(hhfa), accessed 26 May 2024).

indicators and application. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2022 (https://iris.
who.int/handle/10665/364379).

system for service delivery (reference manual, Version 2.2). Geneva: World
Health Organization; 2014 (Revised July 2015) (https://apps.who.int/iris/

Indicator name | Availability of trained health care staff for diabetes management
Purpose | To assess the availability of high-quality services for diabetes management.
Definition | Proportion of health facilities in which staff have been trained in the latest WHO
or national guidelines on diabetes clinical management.
Numerator | Number of health facilities in which staff have been trained in the latest
WHO or national guidelines on diabetes clinical management during the
reporting period.
“Staff” refers to physicians or other nationally authorized health professionals for
diabetes management. A multidisciplinary care team for diabetes management
may include the following:
● cardiologist
● diabetes nurse
● endocrinologist
● general practitioner
● homecare nurse
● nephrologist
● nutritionist
● ophthalmologist
● physiotherapist
● podiatrist
Denominator | Total number of health facilities
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Facility level of care type, provider ownership type (public/private), facility
location type (urban/rural), training topic, type of health professional
Sources of data | Health facility report, health workforce information system or survey
Limitations/comments | Frequency of training depends on the date of the last version of WHO or national
guidelines, as well as the staff turnover at the health care facility.

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 37): Indicator name | Availability of diabetes, cardiovascular disease and hypertension
core medicines
Purpose | To monitor supply of essential medicines for diabetes management.
Definition | Proportion of health facilities that have diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and
hypertension core medicines based on WHO or national treatment guidelines.
Diabetes core medicines include:
● metformin
● sulfonylurea
● insulin
Cardiovascular disease core medicines include:
● aspirin
● beta blockers
● statins
Hypertension core medicines include the following classes of medications:
● angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
● angiotensin-receptor blockers
● long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
● thiazide and thiazide-like agents
Other core medicines may be added to the list as WHO and national guidelines
are updated.
Numerator | Number of health facilities reporting “no stock-out” of diabetes, cardiovascular
disease and hypertension core medicines during the reporting period.
Denominator | Total number of health facilities
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Type of medicine, type of insulin (short-acting human, intermediate acting
human, long-acting analogue), facility level of care type, provider ownership
type (public/private), facility location type (urban/rural).
Sources of data | Health facility medicine stock register, health facility report, logistics information
system or survey
Limitations/comments | In some settings, health facilities do not dispense medicines so the reporting
units may be community medicine dispensaries/pharmacies.
The preferred data source among the sources listed for this indicator depends on
the data source quality in the local context.

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 41): Indicator name | Availability and quality of a diabetes surveillance system
Purpose | To assess the availability of quality and comprehensive surveillance data for
diabetes programme management.
Definition | Country has an established diabetes surveillance system comprising of all
essential components if:
● Country conducts a standardized population-based health survey that
includes availability and quality of diabetes services every 3 to 5 years.
● Country has an electronic, standardized system for recording person- and
facility-level data that includes diabetes, with high level of coverage.
● Country has a type 1 diabetes registry with national level coverage.
● Country conducts regular standardized health facility surveys on
availability of health facility services including diabetes management
services and on capacities of health facilities to provide these services at
required standards of quality, every 1 to 3 years.
● Country has a well-functioning CRVS system for generating reliable
cause-specific mortality data on a routine basis. The International Form
of Medical Certificate of the Cause of Death is completed by certifiers.
The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is used to code the
causes of death. Cause-of-death data are accessible to policy-makers and
researchers.
Numerator | Not applicable
Denominator | Not applicable
Method of estimation | 1. Country can respond “Yes” to the following questions:
● “Does your country conduct a population-based survey that includes
diabetes?”. The country indicates frequency of conducting the population-
based survey (the country is considered to have available a regular
standardized population-based survey that includes diabetes if there are
published survey statistics at least every 3 to 5 years).
● “Does your country have an electronic standardized system for
recording person-and facility-level data that includes diabetes in public
facilities?”(The country is considered to have an electronic standardized
system if it has an electronic type of system that covers more than 50% of
facilities).
● “Does your country have a type 1 diabetes registry?”, indicate
coverage (national, sub-national or others) and type (population- or
hospital-based).
● “Does your country conduct standardized surveys of facilities to assess
availability of health facility services including diabetes management
services and on capacities of health facilities to provide these services
at required standards of quality?” – indicate the year of last facility
survey (The country has available regular standardized health facility
surveys, if there are published survey statistics on availability, readiness,
quality, management, and financing of diabetes management services,
every 1 to 3 years).
Country needs to provide a copy of documents to support their response to
abovementioned questions.

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 42): Method of
estimation (con't) | 2. Availability and quality of national civil registration and vital statistic systems
are assessed through submissions to the WHO mortality database. WHO
collects mortality data, including cause of death, from civil registration
systems in the WHO mortality database through a routine annual call for
data. Data quality is assessed through usability defined as percentage of all
deaths which are registered with meaningful cause-of-death information. The
system is considered to generate reliable cause-specific mortality data on a
routine basis if:
● Data from the five most recent reporting years are, on average, at least
70% usable. Usability is calculated as:
[(Completeness (%))*(1- Deaths assigned to a garbage code (%)].
● At least 5 years of cause-of-death data have been reported to WHO in the
last 10 years.
● The most recent year of data reported to WHO is no more than 5 years old.
The availability and quality of a diabetes surveillance system is validated
by examining documents that describe or evidence the existence of the
abovementioned essential components of a diabetes surveillance system.
The indicator is considered “Yes” if the country has all the essential components
of a diabetes surveillance system.
The indicator is considered “Partially yes” if the country has one or more, but not
all the essential components of a diabetes surveillance system.
The indicator is considered “No” if the country has none of the essential
components of a diabetes surveillance system.
Disaggregation | Type of surveillance system components
Sources of data | NCD country capacity survey, other survey, country report
Limitations/comments | None

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 44): Indicator name | Overweight and obesity assessment
Purpose | To assess the level of overweight and obesity assessment in health facilities.
Definition | Proportion of people who were attending health facilities and assessed for
overweight and obesity using height, weight and/or body mass index (BMI)
measurements.
Numerator | Number of people who were attending health facilities and were assessed for
overweight and obesity using height, weight and/or BMI measurements during
the reporting period.
Denominator | Total number of people who attended health facilities in the reporting period.
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by diabetes status, obesity or overweight
status and individual-level characteristics such as age, sex, race/ethnicity,
comorbidity status, high-risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence
type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.
Sources of data | Health facility patient registers, health records
Limitations/comments | For any comparison over time or with other populations, age
standardization is needed.
Related links | WHO Noncommunicable disease surveillance, monitoring and reporting:
STEPwise approach to NCD risk factor surveillance (STEPS) [website].
Geneva: World Health Organization; 2024 (https://www.who.int/teams/
noncommunicable-diseases/surveillance/systems-tools/steps, accessed
26 May 2024).

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 45): Indicator name | Tobacco use assessment
Purpose | To assess the level of tobacco use assessment
Definition | Proportion of people with diabetes who were attending health facilities and
were assessed for tobacco use by a health professional in the facility during the
reporting period.
Tobacco products include cigarettes, pipes, cigars, cigarillos, waterpipes (hookah,
shisha), bidis, kretek, heated tobacco products, and all forms of smokeless (oral
and nasal) tobacco. Tobacco products exclude products that do not contain
tobacco, such as electronic nicotine delivery system (ENDS) of which e-cigarettes
are a common type, as well as ‘e-cigars’, ‘e-hookahs’, JUUL and ‘e-pipes’.
Currently using means either daily or non-daily (occasional) use at the
time of visit.
The assessment of tobacco use, defined as a series of questions on intensity,
prolongation, type of product and method of consumption, in the current and
in the past.
Numerator | Number of people with diabetes who were attending health facilities and were
assessed for tobacco use during the reporting period
Denominator | Number of people with diabetes who attended health facilities during the
reporting period
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, facility level of care type, provider ownership
type (public/private), and individual-level characteristics such as age, sex, race/
ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence
type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 52): Indicator name | Chronic kidney disease assessment among people with diabetes
Purpose | To assess the level of chronic kidney disease assessment among people with
diabetes in health facilities.
Definition | The proportion of people with diabetes registered in health facilities who were
assessed for diabetic kidney disease based on the following criteria:
● Presence of an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of <60mL/min
per 1.73m2 on at least two occasions, 1 to 3 months apart; and/or
● Presence of albuminuria in at least two urine samples, 1 to 3
months apart.
Urinary albumin excretion can be estimated in a spot urine sample using several
tests (from most preferred to least preferred):
● urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR)
● urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (PCR)
● reagent strip (“dipstick”) urine analysis for albumin or total protein with
automated reading
● reagent strip (“dipstick”) urine analysis for albumin or total protein with
manual reading.
Numerator | Number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities who were assessed
for diabetic chronic kidney disease during the reporting period.
Denominator | Total number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities.
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by facility level of care type, provider
ownership type (public/private), and individual characteristics such as age,
sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-risk groups, socioeconomic status,
residence type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 61): Indicator name | Physical inactivity prevalence
Purpose | To measure the prevalence of physical inactivity among people aged 18
years and over.
Definition | Proportion of people aged 18 years and over who are insufficiently physically
active (i.e. not meeting WHO recommendation on physical activity for health,
which is equivalent to at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity
per week or equivalent).
Throughout a week, including activity for work, during transport and leisure time,
adults should do at least:
● 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity; or
● 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity; or
● an equivalent combination of moderate- and vigorous-intensity physical
activity achieving at least 600 metabolic equivalents (MET)-minutes.
Physical inactivity can be measured using the Global physical activity
questionnaire.
Numerator | Number of respondents aged 18 years and over, who were insufficiently
physically active.
Denominator | Total number of respondents aged 18 years and over.
Method of calculation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by individual characteristics such as age,
sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-risk groups, socioeconomic status,
residence type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.
Sources of data | Nationally or sub-nationally representative population-based surveys with data
on physical activity using standard measurement tool.
Limitations/comments | For any comparison over time or with other populations, age
standardization is needed.

STEPwise approach to NCD risk factor surveillance (STEPS) [website].

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 62): Indicator name | Overweight and obesity prevalence
Purpose | To measure the prevalence of overweight and obesity.
Definition | Proportion of people overweight or obese.
● Criteria for people aged 18 years and over:
● overweight if body mass index (BMI)=25 to <30; obese if BMI>=30.4
● Criteria for school-aged children and adolescents using WHO Growth
reference: overweight if BMI-for-age is greater than 1 standard
deviation (SD) above the median; obese if BMI-for-age is greater than 2
SDs above the median.
● Criterion for children under 5 years of age using WHO Child growth
standards: overweight if weight for height is above 2 SDs from the median.
Numerator | Number of respondents who were classified with overweight or obesity.
Denominator | Total number of respondents
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify individuals with or without diabetes,
by obesity or overweight, individual characteristics such as age, sex, race/
ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence
type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.
Sources of data | Nationally or sub-nationally representative population-based surveys with height
and weight measurement.
Limitations/comments | For any comparison over time or with other populations, age standardization is
needed. Method of assessment of overweight and obesity may vary in countries.
Related links | WHO Noncommunicable disease surveillance, monitoring and reporting:
STEPwise approach to NCD risk factor surveillance (STEPS) [website].
Geneva: World Health Organization; 2024 (https://www.who.int/teams/

26 May 2024).

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 63): Indicator name | Tobacco use prevalence
Purpose | To measure the prevalence of current tobacco use among individuals aged 18
years and over.
Definition | Proportion of people aged 18 years and over who are currently using tobacco
products, including cigarettes, pipes, cigars, cigarillos, waterpipes (hookah,
shisha), bidis, kretek, heated tobacco products, and all forms of smokeless (oral
and nasal) tobacco.
● Tobacco products exclude products that do not contain tobacco, such
as electronic nicotine delivery system (ENDS) of which e-cigarettes are a
common type, as well as ‘e-cigars’, ‘e-hookahs’, JUUL and ‘e-pipes’.
● Currently using means either daily or non-daily (occasional) use at the
time of visit.
Numerator | Number of respondents aged 18 years and over who were current tobacco users.
Denominator | Total number of respondents aged 18 years and over.
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by individuals with or without diabetes,
type of tobacco products, individual characteristics such as age, sex, race/
ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence
type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.
Sources of data | Nationally or sub-nationally representative population-based surveys with a
question regarding current tobacco use.
Limitations/comments | For any comparison over time or with other populations, age
standardization is needed.
Related links | WHO Noncommunicable disease surveillance, monitoring and reporting:
STEPwise approach to NCD risk factor surveillance (STEPS) [website].
Geneva: World Health Organization; 2024 (https://www.who.int/teams/
noncommunicable-diseases/surveillance/systems-tools/steps, accessed
26 May 2024).
Global Adult Tobacco Survey [website]. Geneva: World Health Organization;
2024 (https://www.who.int/teams/noncommunicable-diseases/surveillance/
systems-tools/global-adult-tobacco-survey, accessed 13 August 2024).

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 64): Indicator name | Hypertension prevalence
Purpose | To measure the prevalence of hypertension among people aged 18
years and over.
Definition | Proportion of people aged 18 years and over with raised blood pressure or on
medication for hypertension.
Raised blood pressure criteria:
● systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 mmHg; or
● diastolic blood pressure (DBP) ≥90 mmHg.
Numerator | Number of respondents aged 18 years and over with raised blood pressure or on
medication for hypertension.
Denominator | Total number of respondents aged 18 years and over.
Method of calculation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by individual characteristics such as age,
sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-risk groups, socioeconomic status,
residence type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.
Sources of data | Nationally or sub-nationally representative population-based surveys with blood
pressure measurement.
Limitations/comments | For any comparison over time or with other populations, age
standardization is needed.
Related links | WHO Noncommunicable disease surveillance, monitoring and reporting:
STEPwise approach to NCD risk factor surveillance (STEPS) [website].
Geneva: World Health Organization; 2024 (https://www.who.int/teams/
noncommunicable-diseases/surveillance/systems-tools/steps, accessed
26 May 2024).

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 65): Indicator name | Glycaemic control among people with diabetes based on glycated
haemoglobin (HbA1c)
Purpose | To measure the effectiveness of clinical services for people with diabetes for
achieving glycaemic control.
Definition | Proportion of people living with diabetes with good glycaemic control based on
HbA1c measurement.
Based on WHO guidelines:
Clinical target: <7% (53mmol/mol)
Global target: <8% (64mmol/mol)
● Glycaemic control can be alternatively defined in accordance with
national targets and guidelines.
● This indicator can be derived from population-level surveys or health
facility-based routine data.
Numerator | Population survey data: Number of respondents with diabetes with good
glycaemic control using HbA1c measurement.
Facility data: Number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities with
good glycaemic control using HbA1c measurement at the last clinical visit during
the reporting period, excluding those who were newly diagnosed with less than
three months of treatment.
Denominator | Population survey data: Total number of respondents with diabetes.
Facility data: Total number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities
during the reporting period, excluding those who were newly diagnosed with less
than three months of treatment.
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by type of diabetes, facility level of
care type, provider ownership type (public/private), and individual-level
characteristics such as age, sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-
risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence type (urban/rural), and health
insurance type.
Sources of data | Nationally or sub-nationally representative population-based surveys, with
HbA1c measurement, health facility patient registers, health records.
Limitations/comments | People with unknown status of glycaemic control (e.g. missed appointment/
dropped out) and patients referred to higher-level care facilities during the
reporting quarter will be counted in the denominator and their glycaemic control
status will be counted as not controlled.
Patients known to have transferred to another facility during the reporting
quarter will be counted in the denominator and their last known status prior to
transfer will be used.
For comparison with other health care facilities the indicator needs to be
age-standardized.

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 67): Indicator name | Glycaemic control among people with diabetes based on fasting
plasma glucose
Purpose | To measure the effectiveness of clinical services for people with diabetes for
achieving glycaemic control.
Definition | Proportion of people with diabetes with good glycaemic control based on FPG
measurement.
Based on WHO guidelines:
Clinical target: <126 mg/dl (7 mmol/l)
Global target: <178 mg/dl (9.9 mmol/l)
● Glycaemic control can be alternatively defined in accordance with
national targets and guidelines.
● This indicator can be derived from population-based surveys or health
facility-based routine data.
Numerator | Population survey data: Number of respondents with diabetes with good
glycaemic control using FPG measurement.
Facility data: Number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities with
good glycaemic control using FPG measurement at the last clinical visit during
the reporting period, excluding those who were newly diagnosed with less than
3 months of treatment.
Denominator | Population survey data: Total number of respondents with diabetes.
Facility data: Total number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities
during the reporting period, excluding those who were newly diagnosed with less
than 3 months of treatment.
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by facility level of care type, provider
ownership type (public/private), and individual-level characteristics such as age,
sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-risk groups, socioeconomic status,
residence type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.
Sources of data | Nationally or sub-nationally representative population -based surveys, with FPG
measurement, health facility patient registers, health records.
Limitations/comments | This indicator could be used only for countries with very limited resources, in
which HbA1c is not available or accessible.
People with unknown status of glycaemic control (e.g. missed appointment/
dropped out) and patients referred to higher-level care facilities during the
reporting quarter, will be counted in the denominator and their glycaemic
control status will be counted as not controlled.
Patients known to have transferred to another facility during the reporting
quarter will be counted in the denominator and their last known status prior to
transfer will be used.
For comparison with other health care facilities the indicator needs to be
age-standardized.

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 69): Indicator name | Blood pressure control among people with diabetes
Purpose | To measure effectiveness of clinical services for people with diabetes and raised
blood pressure for achieving blood pressure control.
Definition | Proportion of people with diabetes with good control of blood pressure based on
WHO or national treatment guidelines.
Based on WHO guidelines: BP is considered controlled when SBP <130 mmHg
among people with diabetes.
● Blood pressure control can alternatively be defined in accordance with
national targets and guidelines.
● This indicator can be derived from population-level surveys or health
facility-based routine data.
Numerator | Population survey data: Number of respondents with diabetes, with good control
of blood pressure.
Facility data: Number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities,
with good control of blood pressure at the last clinical visit during the reporting
period, excluding those who were newly diagnosed with raised blood pressure
with less than 3 months of treatment.
Denominator | Facility data: Total number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities
during the reporting period, excluding those who were newly diagnosed with
raised blood pressure with less than three months of treatment.
Population survey data: Total number of respondents with diabetes.
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by type of diabetes, individual
characteristics such as age, sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-
risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence type (urban/rural), and health
insurance type.
Sources of data | Nationally or sub-nationally representative population-based surveys, with
plasma glucose or HbA1c and blood pressure measurement, health facility
patient registers, health records.
Limitations/comments | For any comparison over time or with other populations, age
standardization is needed.
Related links | HEARTS-D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes. Geneva: World Health
Organization; 2020 (https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/331710).

indicators and application. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2022 (https://iris.
who.int/handle/10665/364379).

● This indicator can be derived from population-level surveys or health
facility-based routine data.
Numerator | Population survey data: Number of respondents with diabetes, with good control
of blood pressure.
Facility data: Number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities,
with good control of blood pressure at the last clinical visit during the reporting
period, excluding those who were newly diagnosed with raised blood pressure
with less than 3 months of treatment.
Denominator | Facility data: Total number of people with diabetes registered in health facilities
during the reporting period, excluding those who were newly diagnosed with
raised blood pressure with less than three months of treatment.
Population survey data: Total number of respondents with diabetes.
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by type of diabetes, individual
characteristics such as age, sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-
risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence type (urban/rural), and health
insurance type.
Sources of data | Nationally or sub-nationally representative population-based surveys, with
plasma glucose or HbA1c and blood pressure measurement, health facility
patient registers, health records.
Limitations/comments | For any comparison over time or with other populations, age
standardization is needed.

Purpose | To measure outcome of diabetes prevention interventions.

ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence
type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.

blood glucose measurements and a questionnaire, which investigates receiving
medicines for diabetes.
Limitations/comments | For any comparison over time with other populations, age
standardization is needed.

STEPwise approach to NCD risk factor surveillance (STEPS) [website].

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 72): Indicator name | Hospitalization for diabetes
Purpose | To assess outcome of diabetes management.
Definition | Proportion of people with diabetes who were admitted to hospital due to
following conditions:
1. Severe hypoglycaemia
2. Diabetic ketoacidosis
3. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state
4. Myocardial infarction

7. Kidney failure

during the reporting period.
Denominator | Total number of people with diabetes registered in the facility.

Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by cause of admission, facility level
of care type, provider ownership type (public/private), and individual-level
characteristics such as age, sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-
risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence type (urban/rural), and health
insurance type.
Sources of data | Health facility patient registers, health records

age-standardized.

text:
Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 77): Indicator name | Cardiovascular disease mortality rate
Purpose | To measure impact of diabetes programme.
Definition | Number of cardiovascular disease deaths per 100 000 population.
Numerator | Number of cardiovascular disease deaths in a given period.
Denominator | Total population.
Method of estimation | Numerator ÷ denominator × 100 000
Countries using ICD-10 can include the codes: I00-I99 in the calculation of
cardiovascular disease mortality.
Countries using ICD-11 can include the codes: 8B00-8B2Z, BA00-BE2Z in the
calculation of cardiovascular disease mortality.
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by type of CVD, individual characteristics
such as age, sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-risk groups,
socioeconomic status, residence type (urban/rural), and health insurance type.
Sources of data | Civil registration with complete coverage and medical certification of
cause of death.
Limitations/comments | For any comparison over time or with other populations, age
standardisation is needed.
When calculating deaths by cause using ICD-10, WHO reassigns deaths
assigned to ill-defined causes of death, such as those assigned to signs and
symptoms (R00-R94, R96- R99), heart failure (I50), unspecified cardiac arrest (I46),
and unspecified respiratory failure (J96).
Related links | ICD-11 for mortality and morbidity statistics. Geneva: World Health Organization;
2024 (https://icd.who.int/browse11/l-m/en, accessed 26 May 2024).
WHO methods and data sources for country-level causes of death. Geneva: World
Health Organization; 2020 (https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/374896).

assigned to ill-defined causes of death, such as those assigned to signs and
symptoms (R00-R94, R96- R99), heart failure (I50), unspecified cardiac arrest (I46),
and unspecified respiratory failure (J96).

Guidance on global monitoring for diabetes prevention and control (table, page 79): Indicator name | Probability of premature mortality from noncommunicable diseases
Purpose | To measure impact of diabetes programme.
Definition | Probability of dying between the exact ages 30 and 70 years from cardiovascular
diseases, cancer, diabetes, or chronic respiratory diseases.
Numerator | Not applicable
Denominator | Not applicable
Method of estimation | Probability of death between exact age 30 and exact age 70 are calculated
using cause-specific mortality rates in each 5-year age group and standard
life table methods. The estimates are derived from the WHO Global health
estimates (GHE). These estimates represent the best estimates of WHO,
computed using standard categories, definitions and methods to ensure cross-
country comparability, and may not be the same as official national estimates.
Disaggregation | Where possible and applicable, stratify by type of diabetes, individual
characteristics such as age, sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidity status, high-
risk groups, socioeconomic status, residence type (urban/rural), and health
insurance type.
Sources of data | Civil registration with complete coverage and medical certification of
cause of death.
Limitations/comments | The ICD codes to be included in the calculation are:
cardiovascular disease: I00-I99, Cancer: C00-C97, Diabetes: E10-E14, Chronic
respiratory: J30-J98. When calculating deaths by cause, WHO reassigns deaths
assigned to ill-defined causes of death, such as those assigned to signs and
symptoms (ICD10 codes R00-R94, R96- R99), heart failure (I50), unspecified
cardiac arrest (I46), and unspecified respiratory failure (J96).
